first_draft_paragraphs.text: “MY train got in half an hour ago,” explained Julius, as he led the way out of the station. “I reckoned you’d come by this before I left London, and wired accordingly to Sir James. He’s booked rooms for us, and will be round to dine at eight.”
“What made you think he’d ceased to take any interest in the case?” asked Tommy curiously.
“What he said,” replied Julius dryly. “The old bird’s as close as an oyster! Like all the darned lot of them, he wasn’t going to commit himself till he was sure he could deliver the goods.”
“I wonder,” said Tommy thoughtfully.
Julius turned on him. “You wonder what?”
“Whether that was his real reason.”
“Sure. You bet your life it was.”
Tommy shook his head unconvinced.
Sir James arrived punctually at eight o’clock, and Julius introduced Tommy. Sir James shook hands with him warmly.
“I am delighted to make your acquaintance, Mr. Beresford. I have heard so much about you from Miss Tuppence”--he smiled involuntarily--“that it really seems as though I already know you quite well.”

“Thank you, sir,” said Tommy with his cheerful grin. Like Tuppence, he felt the magnetism of the other’s personality. He was reminded of Mr. Carter. The two men, totally unlike so far as physical resemblance went, produced a similar effect. Beneath the weary manner of the one and the professional reserve of the other, lay the same quality of mind, keen-edged like a rapier.

He was conscious of Sir James’s close scrutiny, and had the feeling that the other had read him through and through like an open book. Sir James took in everything, but gave out only what he chose. A proof of that occurred almost at once.
Julius broke out into a flood of eager questions. How had Sir James managed to track the girl? Why had he not let them know that he was still working on the case?
Sir James stroked his chin and smiled. “Just so, just so. Well, she’s found. And that’s the great thing, isn’t it? Eh! Come now, that’s the great thing?”
“But where is she?” demanded Julius. “I thought you’d be sure to bring her along?”

“That would hardly be possible,” said Sir James gravely. “The young lady was knocked down in a street accident, and has sustained slight injuries to the head. She was taken to the infirmary, and on recovering consciousness gave her name as Jane Finn. When--ah!--I heard that, I arranged for her to be removed to the house of a doctor--a friend of mine, and wired at once for you. She relapsed into unconsciousness and has not spoken since. Her state is probably to be attributed to the mental shock consequent on recovering her memory.”
“It’s come back?” cried Julius excitedly.
Sir James tapped the table rather impatiently. “Undoubtedly, Mr. Hersheimmer, since she was able to give her real name.”
“And you just happened to be on the spot,” said Tommy. “Seems quite like a fairy tale.”
But Sir James was far too wary to be drawn.
“Coincidences are curious things,” he said dryly.

Nevertheless Tommy was now certain of what he had before only suspected. Sir James’s presence in Manchester was not accidental. Far from abandoning the case, as Julius supposed, he had by some means of his own successfully run the missing girl to earth. The only thing that puzzled Tommy was the reason for all this secrecy. He concluded that it was a foible of the legal mind.
“After dinner,” Julius announced, “I shall go right away and see Jane.”
“That will be impossible, I fear,” said Sir James. “It is very unlikely they would allow her to see visitors at this time of night. I should suggest to-morrow morning about ten o’clock.”
Julius flushed. “All the same, I reckon I’ll go round there to-night and see if I can’t ginger them up to break through their silly rules.”
“It will be quite useless, Mr. Hersheimmer.”

The words came out like the crack of a pistol, and Tommy looked up with a start. For a moment the hostility between the two seemed likely to burst into flame, but in the end Julius lowered his eyes, defeated.
“For the moment, I reckon you’re the boss.”

“Thank you,” said the other. “We will say ten o’clock then?” With consummate ease of manner he turned to Tommy. “I must confess, Mr. Beresford, that it was something of a surprise to me to see you here this evening. Miss Tuppence was inclined to think you had got into difficulties.”
“I had, sir!” Tommy grinned reminiscently. “I was never in a tighter place in my life.”
Helped out by questions from Sir James, he gave an abbreviated account of his adventures.
“You got yourself out of a tight place very well,” said the lawyer gravely. “I congratulate you.”
“I couldn’t have got away but for the girl, sir.”
“No.” Sir James smiled a little. “It was lucky for you she happened to--er--take a fancy to you. There’s no doubt about her being one of the gang, I suppose?”
“I’m afraid not, sir. I thought perhaps they were keeping her there by force, but the way she acted didn’t fit in with that. You see, she went back to them when she could have got away.”
Sir James nodded thoughtfully. “What did she say? Something about wanting to be taken to Marguerite?”
“Yes, sir. I suppose she meant Mrs. Vandemeyer.”

“She always signed herself Rita Vandemeyer. All her friends spoke of her as Rita. Still, I suppose the girl must have been in the habit of calling her by her full name. And, at the moment she was crying out to her, Mrs. Vandemeyer was either dead or dying! Curious! There are one or two points that strike me as being obscure--their sudden change of attitude towards yourself, for instance. By the way, the house was raided, of course?”
“Yes, sir, but they’d all cleared out. And not a clue left behind.”
“I wonder----” The lawyer tapped the table thoughtfully.
“I wish you’d been there, sir, to go over the house!” Tommy said impulsively.
“I wish I had,” said Sir James quietly. “And since then? What have you been doing?”
“I forgot that you didn’t know about Tuppence,” Tommy said slowly. The sickening anxiety swept over him again.
The lawyer laid down his knife and fork sharply. “Has anything happened to Miss Tuppence?”
“She’s disappeared,” said Julius.
“When?”
“A week ago.”
Sir James’s questions fairly shot out. Between them Tommy and Julius gave the history of the last week and their futile search.

“A wire signed with your name? They knew enough of you both for that,” said Sir James. “Their kidnapping of Miss Tuppence is the counter-move to your escape. If necessary they could seal your lips with a threat of what might happen to her.”
“That’s just what I thought, sir,” said Tommy.

“You had worked that out, had you? Not bad--not at all bad. The curious thing is that they certainly did not know anything about you when they first held you prisoner. You are sure that you did not in any way disclose your identity?”
Tommy shook his head.
“That’s so,” said Julius with a nod. “Therefore I reckon some one put them wise--and not earlier than Sunday afternoon.”
“Yes, but who?”

“That almighty omniscient Mr. Brown, of course!” There was a faint note of derision in the American’s voice. “I reckon it out that he’s a figurehead--just a bogy name to frighten the children with. The real head of this business is that Russian chap Kramenin.”
“I disagree with you,” said Sir James shortly. “Mr. Brown exists.” He turned to Tommy. “Did you happen to notice where that wire was handed in?”
“No, sir, I’m afraid I didn’t. It’s upstairs, sir, in my kit.”

“I’d like to have a look at it sometime. No hurry. You’ve wasted a week”--Tommy hung his head--“a day or so more is immaterial. We’ll deal with Miss Jane Finn first. I don’t think Miss Tuppence is in any immediate danger. That is, so long as they don’t know that we’ve got Jane Finn, and that her memory has returned. We must keep that dark at all costs.”
At ten o’clock the next morning, Sir James joined the two young men on the doctor’s doorstep. He alone appeared unexcited.
“Mr. Hersheimmer--Mr. Beresford--Dr. Roylance. How’s the patient?”
“Going on well,” said the doctor. “Evidently no idea of the flight of time. Asked this morning how many had been saved from the _Lusitania_. She seems to have something on her mind, though.”

Tommy’s heart beat sensibly faster as they followed the doctor upstairs. Jane Finn at last! If only Tuppence could have been at his side to share in the triumphant conclusion of their joint venture! Then he put the thought resolutely aside. And suddenly a dread clutched at his heart. It seemed too easy.... Suppose they should find her dead ... stricken down by the hand of Mr. Brown?

In another minute he was laughing at these melodramatic fancies. On the white bed, bandages round her head, lay the girl. Somehow the whole scene seemed unreal. It was so exactly what one expected that it gave the effect of being beautifully staged.
“Miss Finn,” said Sir James, “this is your cousin, Mr. Julius P. Hersheimmer.”
“How do, Cousin Jane?” said Julius lightly. But Tommy caught the tremor in his voice.
“Are you really Uncle Hiram’s son?” she asked wonderingly.
Her voice, with the slight warmth of the Western accent, had an almost thrilling quality. It seemed vaguely familiar to Tommy, but he thrust the impression aside as impossible.
“Sure thing.”
“Mother figured it out that Uncle Hiram would never get over being mad with her.”
“The old man was like that,” admitted Julius. “But I guess the new generation’s sort of different. Got no use for the family feud business.”

A shadow passed over the girl’s face. “They’ve been telling me things--dreadful things--that my memory went, and that there are years I shall never know about--years lost out of my life. It seems to me as though it were no time since we were being hustled into those boats.”

“Don’t worry any,” said Julius. “Now, see here, Jane, there was a man aboard that boat with some mighty important papers on him.” As her glance shifted to the others, he added: “Mr. Beresford is commissioned by the British Government to get those papers back, and it’s owing to Sir James that we’ve ferreted you out at last. Did Danvers give you the papers?”
“Yes. He said they’d have a better chance with me, because they would save the women and children first.”
“Just as we thought,” said Sir James.
“Then you can hand them over to us right away?” said Julius.
“But I can’t. I haven’t got them.”
“You--haven’t--got them?”
“No--I hid them. I got uneasy. People seemed to be watching me.”
“Go on,” said Sir James, in his quiet penetrating tones. “What do you remember?”

“It was at Holyhead. In the confusion on the quay I slipped away. I took a car. Told the man to drive me out of the town. No other car was following us. I saw a path at the side of the road. I told the man to wait.

“The path led to the cliff, and down to the sea between big yellow gorse bushes--they were like golden flames. There wasn’t a soul in sight. But just level with my head there was a hole in the rock. It was quite small--I could only just get my hand in, but it went a long way back. I took the oilskin packet from round my neck and shoved it right in as far as I could. Then I tore off a bit of gorse--My! but it did prick--and plugged the hole with it so that you’d never guess there was a crevice of any kind there. There was a queer boulder in the path just there--for all the world like a dog sitting up begging. Then I went back to the road and just caught the train. By and by, I saw the man opposite me wink at a woman who was sitting next to me, and I felt scared again, and was glad the papers were safe. I went out in the corridor. But the woman called me back, said I’d dropped something, and when I stooped to look, something seemed to hit me--here.” She placed her hand to the back of her head. “I don’t remember anything more until I woke up in the hospital.”
“Thank you, Miss Finn,” said Sir James. “I hope we have not tired you?”
“Oh, that’s all right. My head aches a little, but otherwise I feel fine.”
Julius stepped forward and took her hand again.

“So long, Cousin Jane. I’m going to get busy after those papers, but I’ll be back in two shakes of a dog’s tail, and I’ll tote you up to London and give you the time of your young life before we go back to the States! I mean it--so hurry up and get well.”

London and give you the time of your young life before we go back to the
States! I mean it--so hurry up and get well.”

preservation_plan.book_context: A 1919-era thriller structured as alternating threads: Tommy's captivity, Tuppence's investigations, and Julius's hustle. Every chapter plants clues that pay off in the final unmasking. Recurring mechanisms include bluffing with ignorance, telegrams and notes as decoys, concealment between allies ('Never tell all you know'), and the Mr. Brown motif of an ordinary, unseen chief. Chapters XVI–XIX carry the plot from Tommy's bluff in the Soho house, through his escape with the help of 'Annette', to the bogus telegram that lures Tuppence away and Sir James's 'discovery' of Jane Finn in Manchester. These chapters seed several later reveals: the Faust picture as hiding place, the Marguerite cry, Annette as the real Jane, Charing Cross versus the altered telegram, the 'Twopence' signature test, the Sunday timing of Tommy's exposure, the staged Manchester girl, and Sir James as Mr. Brown. The abridgment must keep these clues present but unexplained in the chapters where they first appear.
continuity_checks: The girl is presented as Jane Finn without narrative contradiction. Only the 'staged' and 'familiar voice' hints remain.
No suggestion that Sir James is Mr. Brown. His attentiveness must read as possible genuine diligence.
Julius's attraction to Jane is not resolved here; his later 'cured' confession comes in the next chapter.
Jane's account says she took the oilskin packet from round her neck. Do not alter it to match the later true story.
Sir James says he cannot accompany them only in the next chapter. Do not anticipate it.

essential: Julius explains the arrangements. Tommy doubts that 'close as an oyster' is the real reason for Sir James's silence.
Sir James meets Tommy and mentions hearing of him from Tuppence. Tommy feels his magnetism and compares him to Carter. Sir James 'took in everything, but gave out only what he chose'.
Julius demands to know how the girl was found. Sir James evades.

Sir James's account: a street accident, the infirmary, the girl giving her name as Jane Finn, her removal to a doctor friend's house. Her memory has returned. Tommy's 'like a fairy tale' meets 'Coincidences are curious things'.
Tommy concludes that Sir James never abandoned the case and attributes the secrecy to legal habit.
The clash over visiting that night: Sir James's pistol-crack 'quite useless', and Julius backing down ('you're the boss').

Tommy's abbreviated adventures. Sir James praises him and suggests Annette 'took a fancy' to him. Tommy concedes she seems one of the gang because she went back. Sir James comments on 'Marguerite' versus Rita, notes the gang's sudden change of attitude, and wishes he had searched the house.

Tuppence's disappearance comes out. Sir James's keen questions; the kidnapping is a counter-move and Tommy had worked that out. Tommy was unknown when first held. Julius times the leak to Sunday afternoon and dismisses Mr. Brown as a bogy in favour of Kramenin. Sir James insists Mr. Brown exists and asks where the wire was handed in. He wants to see it, rebukes the wasted week, and says Jane's recovery must be kept dark.
At the doctor's house, Dr. Roylance says she asked about the Lusitania survivors. On the stairs Tommy longs for Tuppence and has a fleeting dread. The scene seems 'beautifully staged'.
Julius and Jane: 'Uncle Hiram', the feud, her lost years. Her voice seems familiar to Tommy. Julius reassures her about the others.

Jane confirms Danvers gave her the papers. Her account: Holyhead, slipping away by car, the cliff path through golden gorse, the hole plugged with gorse, the begging-dog boulder, the wink on the train, the blow.
Julius promises to return and to give her 'the time of your young life'.

preservation_plan.voice_profile: Brisk, ironic third-person narration that stays close to Tommy, and later to Tommy and Julius, in the 'Young Adventurers' manner. The comedy comes from undercutting: Tommy's flippant, schoolboy bravado ('old bean', mock-heroic asides, 'Retire, varlet') is set against honest admissions of fear ('glad they could not hear the persistent beating of his heart'). Narrative generalisation about types ('one of those young Englishmen...') and cinema or dime-novel self-consciousness recur. Dialogue does most of the work. National idiom marks each speaker: Julius's Americanisms ('Put me wise', 'Sure thing', 'gets my goat'), the German's clipped menace, Conrad's and Number 14's cockney, Annette's broken English and French. Sir James speaks in dry, evasive legal phrasing ('Coincidences are curious things'). Chapters end on hooks: a reversal, a telegram, a twist. Double-hyphen dashes, '----' for broken-off speech and underscore emphasis are characteristic and must be retained.
